title: Trump calls AI oversight push a 'SICK conspiracy,' rejects slowdown call
subtitle: Days after Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI leaders asked for a pause, the president posted that AI risk is a 'HOAX' and compared safety advocates to climate scientists.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: President Donald Trump on Monday, September 14, 2026, publicly rejected the coordinated call from Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk to slow frontier AI development. In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote that "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX" and called the push for guardrails a "SICK conspiracy" against AI and data centers. He compared safety advocates to climate scientists — which he also called a hoax — and said the country needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president to keep the buildout going.

The post matters because it closes off, for now, one of the two paths a lab-led slowdown would need to work. Amodei's Saturday essay implicitly assumes either that Washington will impose a pace limit, or that voluntary coordination will hold long enough for safety research to catch up. Trump just told the labs the first path is off. Whether the second path can hold when rivals face investor pressure to keep shipping is the question the next earnings cycle will answer.

The White House posture also complicates the joint safety body that Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have been quietly discussing since July. A self-regulator without government backing is exposed to antitrust risk when competitors write rules together. A self-regulator with an administration that has called the underlying concern a hoax has no political cover if a member firm sues to overturn a rule. Governor-level statutes in California, Colorado, and Illinois remain on the books, but the December 2025 executive order stood up a Justice Department AI Litigation Task Force whose stated job is to challenge state AI laws.

For learners: US AI policy right now runs on three tracks — federal deregulation, state-by-state statutes, and voluntary industry commitments — and they contradict each other. When a headline says "AI is regulated" or "AI is unregulated," ask which track. A model deployed in California under state law, sold to a federal contractor under an executive order, and audited by a voluntary industry body sits inside all three at once. Reading policy news is easier once you know that the layers are not stacked, they are competing.
